# Tutorial 05: Internal Rate of Return

## Exercise 1: The Espresso Machine

Café Kurbel, a bicycle repair shop that discovered it earns more from coffee than from inner tubes, wants to buy a commercial espresso machine for **€12,000**. The owners expect net cash inflows of **€3,000 per year** for five years and a resale value of **€2,000** at the end of year 5. Their cost of capital is **8%**.

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $CF_t$ (€) | −12,000 | 3,000 | 3,000 | 3,000 | 3,000 | 3,000 + 2,000 |

#### Task 1: NPV at the cost of capital

Compute the NPV of the machine at 8%. Should Café Kurbel invest?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Given: $I_0 = 12{,}000$; $CF_t = 3{,}000$ for $t = 1, \dots, 5$; $L_5 = 2{,}000$; $i = 8\%$.

The inflows form an ordinary annuity, so use the PVIFA and discount the resale value separately:

$$
C_0(8\%) = -12{,}000 + 3{,}000 \cdot PVIFA(8\%, 5) + \frac{2{,}000}{1.08^5} = -12{,}000 + 3{,}000 \cdot 3.99271 + 1{,}361.17
$$

$$
= -12{,}000 + 11{,}978.13 + 1{,}361.17 = 1{,}339.30
$$

The NPV is positive: **invest**. The machine creates €1,339.30 of value beyond the 8% alternative.
:::

#### Task 2: IRR by iteration and linear interpolation

Find the IRR of the machine. Compute the NPV at 10%, 11% and 12%, bracket the IRR between two neighbouring rates and interpolate linearly (Regula Falsi). Compare the result with the hurdle rate.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

$C_0(i) = -12{,}000 + 3{,}000 \cdot PVIFA(i, 5) + 2{,}000 \cdot (1+i)^{-5}$

| Trial rate $i$ | $PVIFA(i, 5)$ | PV of annuity (€) | PV of resale (€) | $C_0(i)$ (€) |
|:---:|:---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10% | 3.7908 | 11,372.36 | 1,241.84 | +614.20 |
| 11% | 3.6959 | 11,087.69 | 1,186.90 | +274.59 |
| 12% | 3.6048 | 10,814.33 | 1,134.85 | −50.82 |

The sign changes between 11% and 12%, so $i_1 = 11\%$, $i_2 = 12\%$:

$$
r \approx 0.11 + \frac{274.59}{274.59 - (-50.82)} \cdot (0.12 - 0.11) = 0.11 + \frac{274.59}{325.41} \cdot 0.01 = 0.1184
$$

$r \approx 11.84\%$ (exact: 11.84%). Since $r = 11.84\% > i = 8\%$, the IRR rule also says **invest** — as it must for a conventional investment with a positive NPV.

**Grading Notes:** Accept any bracket of width 1 percentage point that contains the IRR; interpolation over a wider bracket (e.g. 10% to 12%) gives a slightly higher estimate (about 11.85%) and is acceptable if the direction of the error is explained.
:::

#### Task 3: Modified IRR

The owners will park every euro the machine earns in the café's investment account at 8%. Compute the MIRR at 8% and explain in one or two sentences why it is lower than the IRR.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Compound every inflow to $t = 5$ at 8%:

| $t$ | Inflow (€) | Factor $1.08^{5-t}$ | Value at $t = 5$ (€) |
|:---:|---:|:---:|---:|
| 1 | 3,000 | 1.3605 | 4,081.47 |
| 2 | 3,000 | 1.2597 | 3,779.14 |
| 3 | 3,000 | 1.1664 | 3,499.20 |
| 4 | 3,000 | 1.0800 | 3,240.00 |
| 5 | 5,000 | 1.0000 | 5,000.00 |
| | | $TV_5$ | **19,599.80** |

The only outflow is $I_0$, so $PV_{out} = 12{,}000$:

$$
MIRR = \left(\frac{19{,}599.80}{12{,}000}\right)^{1/5} - 1 = 1.6333^{0.2} - 1 = 10.31\%
$$

The MIRR (10.31%) lies between the cost of capital (8%) and the IRR (11.84%). Reading the IRR as the growth rate of the €12,000 over five years would require every €3,000 released by the machine to earn 11.84% as well; in the investment account it earns only 8%, so the realised return on the whole investment is lower.
:::

## Exercise 2: Two Mowers, One Lawn

Grünschnitt GbR, a two-person landscaping business, needs one new mower — not two. The compact model (A) is cheap and pays back quickly; the ride-on model (B) costs more but lets the team take on larger contracts. Both last two years and have no resale value. The partners borrow at **6%**.

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| A: Compact mower (€) | −20,000 | 15,000 | 10,000 |
| B: Ride-on mower (€) | −50,000 | 24,000 | 38,000 |

#### Task 1: NPV of both mowers

Compute the NPV of A and B at 6%. Which mower does the NPV rule favour?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Discount factors: $1.06^{-1} = 0.9434$, $1.06^{-2} = 0.8900$.

$$
C_0^{A} = -20{,}000 + \frac{15{,}000}{1.06} + \frac{10{,}000}{1.06^2} = -20{,}000 + 14{,}150.94 + 8{,}899.96 = 3{,}050.91
$$

$$
C_0^{B} = -50{,}000 + \frac{24{,}000}{1.06} + \frac{38{,}000}{1.06^2} = -50{,}000 + 22{,}641.51 + 33{,}819.86 = 6{,}461.37
$$

Both are acceptable on their own; the NPV rule favours **B** (€6,461.37 > €3,050.91).
:::

#### Task 2: Exact IRRs with the quadratic formula

For a two-year project the IRR equation is a quadratic equation in $q = 1 + r$. Multiply $C_0(r) = 0$ by $q^2$ and solve for $q$ with the quadratic formula. Compute the IRRs of A and B. Which mower does the IRR comparison favour?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Multiplying $-I_0 + CF_1/q + CF_2/q^2 = 0$ by $q^2$ gives $I_0 q^2 - CF_1 q - CF_2 = 0$, with the positive root

$$
q = \frac{CF_1 + \sqrt{CF_1^2 + 4 \cdot I_0 \cdot CF_2}}{2 \cdot I_0}
$$

Project A: $20{,}000 q^2 - 15{,}000 q - 10{,}000 = 0$

$$
q_A = \frac{15{,}000 + \sqrt{15{,}000^2 + 4 \cdot 20{,}000 \cdot 10{,}000}}{40{,}000} = \frac{15{,}000 + 32{,}015.62}{40{,}000} = 1.1754 \;\Rightarrow\; r_A = 17.54\%
$$

Project B: $50{,}000 q^2 - 24{,}000 q - 38{,}000 = 0$

$$
q_B = \frac{24{,}000 + \sqrt{24{,}000^2 + 4 \cdot 50{,}000 \cdot 38{,}000}}{100{,}000} = \frac{24{,}000 + 90{,}421.24}{100{,}000} = 1.1442 \;\Rightarrow\; r_B = 14.42\%
$$

The IRR comparison favours **A** (17.54% > 14.42%) — the opposite of the NPV ranking. (The second root of each equation is negative in $q$ and has no economic meaning; one sign change means exactly one positive root.)
:::

#### Task 3: Incremental investment and crossover rate

Form the incremental investment B − A. Compute its NPV at 6% and its IRR (quadratic formula again). Which mower should Grünschnitt buy?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| $\Delta CF_t$ = B − A (€) | −30,000 | 9,000 | 28,000 |

$$
C_0^{\Delta}(6\%) = -30{,}000 + \frac{9{,}000}{1.06} + \frac{28{,}000}{1.06^2} = -30{,}000 + 8{,}490.57 + 24{,}919.90 = 3{,}410.47
$$

Check: $C_0^{B} - C_0^{A} = 6{,}461.37 - 3{,}050.91 = 3{,}410.46$ (difference of 0.01 from rounding).

IRR of the increment: $30{,}000 q^2 - 9{,}000 q - 28{,}000 = 0$

$$
q_\Delta = \frac{9{,}000 + \sqrt{9{,}000^2 + 4 \cdot 30{,}000 \cdot 28{,}000}}{60{,}000} = \frac{9{,}000 + 58{,}660.04}{60{,}000} = 1.1277 \;\Rightarrow\; r_\Delta = 12.77\%
$$

The extra €30,000 for the ride-on mower earns 12.77%, more than the 6% it costs. **Buy B.** The crossover rate of the two NPV functions is 12.77%: below it B has the higher NPV, above it A.
:::

#### Task 4: When the bank gets greedy

The bank raises the partners' borrowing rate to **15%**. Without changing the cash flows, decide again — first using the crossover rate, then confirm with both NPVs.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

At 15% the cost of capital lies above the crossover rate of 12.77%, so the increment B − A no longer pays and **A becomes the better choice**.

$$
C_0^{A}(15\%) = -20{,}000 + \frac{15{,}000}{1.15} + \frac{10{,}000}{1.15^2} = 604.91, \qquad
C_0^{B}(15\%) = -50{,}000 + \frac{24{,}000}{1.15} + \frac{38{,}000}{1.15^2} = -396.98
$$

B is now not even acceptable on its own ($r_B = 14.42\% < 15\%$), while A still is. The IRRs are the same as in Task 2; only the hurdle moved — which is exactly why the IRRs alone could not decide.
:::

## Exercise 3: Sign Patterns and Traps

#### Task 1: Multiple choice — IRR, MIRR and sign changes

Which of the following statements are **correct**? (Multiple answers possible.)

a) A conventional investment (one outflow at $t = 0$, inflows thereafter) has exactly one IRR greater than −100%.

b) A project whose cash flows change sign twice always has two IRRs.

c) If two mutually exclusive projects are ranked differently by IRR and by NPV, the NPV ranking at the cost of capital is the one to follow.

d) Computing the MIRR at the cost of capital removes the scale problem when ranking projects of different size.

e) Linear interpolation between two trial rates that bracket the IRR slightly overestimates the IRR of a conventional investment.

f) For a financing profile (inflow first, outflows later), the deal is attractive when its IRR exceeds the cost of capital.

g) All statements are false.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:** Correct are **a)**, **c)** and **e)**.

- **a) Correct.** One sign change means exactly one positive root $q = 1 + r$ (Descartes' rule of signs), i.e. one IRR above −100%. It is positive only if the undiscounted cash flows exceed the investment.
- **b) Incorrect.** Two sign changes allow two IRRs *or none*; Descartes gives a ceiling, not a count (e.g. −100, +250, −165 has no IRR).
- **c) Correct.** The NPV measures the value created in euros; the incremental investment reproduces the NPV ranking.
- **d) Incorrect.** The MIRR repairs the reinvestment distortion, not the scale problem — 15% on €100,000 is still less wealth than 12% on €300,000.
- **e) Correct.** The NPV function of a conventional investment is convex, so the straight chord crosses zero slightly to the right of the true IRR.
- **f) Incorrect.** For a financing profile the IRR is the cost of the borrowing; it is attractive when $r < i$.
- **g) Incorrect**, since a), c) and e) are correct.
:::

#### Task 2: Transfer — the bigger pump

An oil producer considers replacing its pump with a bigger one that empties the same field faster. Compared with keeping the old pump, the bigger pump costs €1,600 extra today, brings €10,000 of oil forward into year 1 and therefore means €10,000 *less* oil revenue in year 2. The cost of capital is 10%.

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Incremental $CF_t$ (€) | −1,600 | 10,000 | −10,000 |

a) Show that both 25% and 400% are IRRs of this incremental project.

b) Compute the NPV at 10% and decide.

c) Explain in two or three sentences why the IRR rule cannot make this decision and what you would report instead if management insists on a percentage.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

**a)** At $r = 25\%$: $-1{,}600 + \frac{10{,}000}{1.25} - \frac{10{,}000}{1.25^2} = -1{,}600 + 8{,}000 - 6{,}400 = 0$.
At $r = 400\%$: $-1{,}600 + \frac{10{,}000}{5} - \frac{10{,}000}{25} = -1{,}600 + 2{,}000 - 400 = 0$.
Both rates set the NPV to zero. The sequence $-, +, -$ has two sign changes, so Descartes' rule allows exactly this: two IRRs.

**b)**

$$
C_0(10\%) = -1{,}600 + \frac{10{,}000}{1.10} - \frac{10{,}000}{1.10^2} = -1{,}600 + 9{,}090.91 - 8{,}264.46 = -773.55
$$

The NPV is negative: **keep the old pump**. Bringing the oil forward by one year is worth only €826.45 at 10% — less than the €1,600 the bigger pump costs.

**c)** Both IRRs lie above the 10% hurdle, so a mechanical "IRR above hurdle" rule would accept the pump — wrongly. The NPV is positive only for discount rates between 25% and 400% and negative at the firm's actual cost of capital; with two sign changes, no single IRR describes the project's return. If management wants a percentage, report the MIRR at 10% (outflows discounted to $t = 0$, inflows compounded to $t = 2$): $\left(\frac{10{,}000 \cdot 1.10}{1{,}600 + 10{,}000/1.10^2}\right)^{1/2} - 1 = \left(\frac{11{,}000}{9{,}864.46}\right)^{1/2} - 1 = 5.60\%$, which is unique and below 10%, consistent with the negative NPV.

**Grading Notes:** Full marks for c) require (1) the observation that both IRRs exceed the hurdle yet the NPV is negative and (2) a sensible alternative (NPV decision, or MIRR as the communicable percentage).
:::
